# Orca CLI and development reference

_This is the CLI and development reference, moved verbatim from the README on 2026-10-03; the README now covers the Web panel._

## Commands

`orca <domain> <action> [ids] [--flags]`; `orca help <domain> [<action>]` prints the same from the registry. Agents: the orca-control skill's references.

### `orca status`

- `orca status` — one screen: is the panel answering, and the facts around it (read-only, starts nothing)

### `orca doctor`

- `orca doctor` — status's checks plus slower ones (agent CLIs on the service PATH, ~/.orca modes, stale sockets), with one fix line per failure (read-only)

### `orca version`

- `orca version` — the CLI's version (the orca-control skill's version: should equal it)

### `orca login`

- `orca login --name <name>` — store a person token for this terminal: the panel account's password, typed here; used only with --as-person

### `orca logout`

- `orca logout` — revoke the stored person token and remove it

### `orca help`

- `orca help [<topic>...]` — this list, or one domain's or one command's help

### `orca project`

- `orca project list` — the registered projects, their roots and control repository ids
- `orca project show` — the project's workspace mode and integration settings (and their revision)
- `orca project set-workspace-mode --mode <mode>` — worktree or clone for the project's runs
- `orca project set-integration --delivery <delivery> [--trigger <trigger>] [--method <method>] [--target <target>] [--remote <remote>]` — where the project's finished work goes by default
- `orca project set-criteria-review [--on] [--off]` — whether Orca's reviewer judges a flagged test change before a person sees it
- `orca project register-plan <path>` — register (or re-trust) a git-tracked plan file of the project so it can be imported

### `orca group`

- `orca group list` — every group: id, state, revision, goal
- `orca group show <group>` — one group's full view
- `orca group import [<plan>] [--group <group>] [--estimator-profile <estimator-profile>] [--estimate-mode <estimate-mode>] [--library <library>] [--version <version>]` — import a registered plan, or a plan library version (--library), as a new draft group
- `orca group estimate <group> [--estimator-profile <estimator-profile>] [--mode <mode>]` — ask the estimator for budgets at the current proposal version
- `orca group confirm <group> [--hold] [--budget-mode <budget-mode>] [--worker-profile <worker-profile>] [--handoff-profile <handoff-profile>] [--goal-review-profile <goal-review-profile>] [--handoff-at-context-tokens <handoff-at-context-tokens>]` — confirm the task plan as shown now; it starts when a slot is free unless --hold
- `orca group start <group>` — start a confirmed group (one confirmed with --hold)
- `orca group pause <group>` — stop dispatching new runs (running ones finish)
- `orca group resume <group>` — dispatch again after a pause
- `orca group stop-handoff <group> [--deadline <deadline>]` — stop: running tasks hand off and stop
- `orca group resume-handoff <group> [--continue <continue>]` — resume after a completed handoff; --continue <task> continues that task from its checkpoint
- `orca group archive <group>` — archive a group: records stay, it refuses every command but unarchive
- `orca group unarchive <group>` — unarchive a group
- `orca group set-limit <group> --limit <limit>` — set the group's budget limit (person token)
- `orca group set-integration <group> --delivery <delivery> [--trigger <trigger>] [--method <method>] [--target <target>] [--remote <remote>]` — where this group's finished work goes
- `orca group retry-integration <group>` — a blocked or conflicted integration back to idle
- `orca group resolve-integration <group>` — approve an agent resolving the group's integration conflict
- `orca group folder-change <group> [--take-folder] [--recheck] [--withhold] [--dir <dir>]` — answer a folder change that stopped placement: --take-folder, --recheck or --withhold (person token)
- `orca group multi-land <group> [--retry-rest] [--mark-resolved]` — answer a stopped multi-directory landing: --retry-rest or --mark-resolved (person token)
- `orca group depend <group> --on <on>` — make the group wait until --on <group> has landed
- `orca group undepend <group> --on <on>` — remove that wait
- `orca group schedule <group> --cron <cron> [--token-limit <token-limit>] [--name <name>] [--disabled] [--id <id>]` — schedule this group from its archived plan: one library version pins the fires; needs a person token (person token)

### `orca requirement`

- `orca requirement show <group>` — a requirement's rounds, drafts and document
- `orca requirement open --idea <idea> [--group <group>] [--language <language>] [--limit <limit>]` — open a requirement from an idea; the group id is generated unless --group names one
- `orca requirement answer <group> [--answer <answer>] [--glossary <glossary>] [--adr <adr>]` — answer the current round: --answer <qid> takes the recommendation, --answer <qid>=<text> answers in words
- `orca requirement consensus <group>` — close clarification at the current round
- `orca requirement continue <group>` — grant exactly one more clarification round after the cap
- `orca requirement revise <group> --round <round> --file <file>` — revise an answered clarification round (a new round; at most one clarify call)
- `orca requirement feedback <group> --text <text>` — ask for a new draft of the split
- `orca requirement accept <group>` — accept the current draft: the group becomes a draft task group
- `orca requirement classify <group> --scope <scope> --clarity <clarity>` — set the requirement's class (it sets the clarification caps)

### `orca proposal`

- `orca proposal show <group>` — the group's budget proposal: version, allocations, group limit, revision
- `orca proposal set-budget <group> [--task <task>] [--allocation <allocation>] [--goal-review] --dimension <dimension> --value <value> [--proposed-group-limit <proposed-group-limit>]` — set one budget value: --task <t> --allocation work|handoff, or --goal-review; --dimension; --value <n>|none
- `orca proposal set-agent <group> [--slot <slot>] [--task <task>] [--agent <agent>] [--model <model>] [--clear]` — set one agent selection layer (--slot worker|estimator|reconcile, or --task <t>); --clear removes it
- `orca proposal replace <group> --file <file>` — send a whole operation list {operations, proposedGroupLimit?} from a file; refused without --if-revision
- `orca proposal edit <group>` — TTY only: edit the proposal in $EDITOR; the changed values are sent as replace --if-revision <the revision read>

### `orca task`

- `orca task show <group> <task>` — one task of a group and its runs
- `orca task retry <group> <task>` — start again a task whose current run failed (the run read now is the one retried)
- `orca task continue <group> <task>` — continue a task's current run from its newest complete checkpoint
- `orca task set-loop <group> <task> --file <file>` — set a task's loop plan from a JSON file {plan,inputs,work,workProvenance?,skills?}
- `orca task set-labels <group> <task> [--label <label>] [--clear]` — set a task's labels (--label repeatable), or --clear back to the plan's
- `orca task verify-saved-result <group> <task>` — verify the current run's saved result instead of re-running (after run eligibility says eligible)
- `orca task settle-usage <group> <task> --acknowledge <acknowledge>` — settle a run's unknown usage (cannot be undone) (person token)

### `orca run`

- `orca run show <run> [--group <group>]` — one run: its entry in the group view, the newest 10 activity rows, the evidence summary
- `orca run activity <run>` — a run's newest 200 activity rows, newest first
- `orca run evidence <run>` — a run's evidence manifest
- `orca run results <run>` — a run's saved results
- `orca run eligibility <run>` — whether a run's saved result can be verified instead of re-run

### `orca decision`

- `orca decision list <group>` — a group's landed, pending and unlanded decisions
- `orca decision approve <group> <id> --undo-how <undo-how>` — approve a decision a landing refused, with an executable undo.how
- `orca decision reject <group> <id> [--because <because>]` — reject a decision a landing refused (records a correction)
- `orca decision ratify <group> <id> [--note <note>]` — accept a landed decision Orca flagged (dismiss a review finding, with --note saying why)
- `orca decision validate <path>...` — validate ledger file(s) or a directory (its top-level *.jsonl only)
- `orca decision metrics [--root <root>] [--repo <repo>] [--as-of <as-of>]` — read-only: the correction rate, the repair rate and the backlog (--json: the report as JSON)
- `orca decision compact-reviews [--apply] [--root <root>] [--repo <repo>]` — compact the reviews store: a dry-run report, or --apply

### `orca correction`

- `orca correction list` — every recorded correction, its debug groups and closed state
- `orca correction record [--decision <decision>] [--run <run>] --kind <kind> --because <because> [--chose-instead <chose-instead>] [--again]` — record a correction of a decision, a run (--run) or, with neither, the project
- `orca correction close <correction> --undo-how <undo-how> [--chose-instead <chose-instead>] [--undo-cost <undo-cost>] [--undo-blast-radius <undo-blast-radius>]` — close a correction by hand with its undo.how
- `orca correction withdraw <correction>` — withdraw a correction
- `orca correction debug <correction> [--reopen] [--check <check>] [--undo-how <undo-how>]` — open the correction's debug group (spends nothing); --reopen for the next one

### `orca agent`

- `orca agent list` — the agent installations the panel can run
- `orca agent models <installation>` — an installation's models
- `orca agent set-preferences [--file <file>] [--review <review>]` — set the operator's agent preferences from a JSON file, or only the model review's agent (--review)
- `orca agent apply-update --accept <accept>` — apply the detected installation changes named by --accept (person token)
- `orca agent init` — detect the installed agents (ccloop agents detect) and write the installation table; an existing table is never overwritten (the detection goes to <table>.draft.json)
- `orca agent show` — validate the installation table and print what each installation resolves to; exit 1 if any entry is refused
- `orca agent refresh` — record the version each installed CLI answers now in the table (only the version fields change)

### `orca usage`

- `orca usage show [--scope <scope>] [--from <from>] [--to <to>] [--group-by <group-by>]` — tokens used per model, the caps and the spend revision
- `orca usage set-cap --scope <scope> --period <period> --tokens <tokens>` — set a spend cap (person token)
- `orca usage clear-cap --scope <scope> --period <period>` — clear a spend cap (person token)
- `orca usage set-calendar --time-zone <time-zone> --week-start <week-start>` — the usage calendar's time zone and first weekday (person token)

### `orca orchestration`

- `orca orchestration show` — how many groups run at once, and how many hold a slot now
- `orca orchestration set --max-running-groups <max-running-groups> [--criteria-review <criteria-review>] [--quota-wait <quota-wait>]` — how many groups run at once; the reviewer default; quota-wait installations

### `orca recovery`

- `orca recovery list` — what blocks dispatch: global, group and run blockers
- `orca recovery retry [--run <run>] [--group <group>] [--acknowledge <acknowledge>]` — resume a run (--run) or a group (--group) blocked for a reason other than a terminal failure

### `orca command`

- `orca command show <commandId> [--group <group>] [--operator] [--spend] [--corrections] [--orchestration]` — a command's retained result, looked up under its scope
- `orca command retry --request <request>` — for an uncertain outcome: look the request up first; resend its exact bytes only on a confirmed miss

### `orca check`

- `orca check show [--global]` — the effective check settings, where each value comes from, locks, scheduled checks and each check's state
- `orca check findings <review>` — a model review's record: range, groups, valid findings, dropped findings with reasons
- `orca check set <kind> [--global] [--on] [--off] [--trigger <trigger>] [--command <command>] [--no-command] [--budget-tokens <budget-tokens>] [--max-groups <max-groups>]` — set a check kind's fields in this project (or --global); --command and --budget-tokens need a person token
- `orca check reset <kind> <field>... [--global]` — remove a kind's fields from this project (or --global) so the next layer applies
- `orca check schedule <id> [--global] [--kind <kind>] [--cron <cron>] [--off] [--remove]` — add, replace or remove a scheduled check in this project (or --global); adding or enabling one needs a person token
- `orca check lock [--lock <lock>]` — set the global lock list (needs a person token); no --lock clears every lock (person token)
- `orca check run <kind>` — run a check kind now in this project (ignores its trigger; still waits for a run in flight and skips an empty range)
- `orca check resume <kind>` — re-arm a check kind paused after three errored runs in this project

### `orca flow`

- `orca flow settings show [--global]` — the effective flow settings of this project (or --global): each value, where it comes from, and its lock
- `orca flow settings set <field> <value> [--global]` — set one flow setting in this project (or --global); needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow settings clear <field>... [--global]` — remove flow settings from this project (or --global) so the next layer applies; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow settings lock <field>` — lock one global flow setting (needs a person token): a locked field may only be tightened in a project (person token)
- `orca flow settings unlock <field>` — unlock one global flow setting (needs a person token): a locked field may only be tightened in a project (person token)
- `orca flow start <template> --dir <dir> [--project <project>] [--param <param>] [--clarify <clarify>] [--pool <pool>] [--unattended]` — start a flow from a built-in template on a folder (--pool needs a person token)
- `orca flow list` — every flow run with its template, state and pool
- `orca flow show <run>` — one flow run: steps with their active and newest execution, open asks, plans, effect records, decisions
- `orca flow journal <run>` — one flow run's every execution and message
- `orca flow feedback <run> [--step <step>] [--execution <execution>] [--quote <quote>] [--heading <heading>] [--paragraph <paragraph>] [--attach <attach>] [--replaces <replaces>] [--hit <hit>] [--as-is] --text <text>` — feedback on the run, a step or one execution: code locates the passage, the model picks the steps that take it, a plan says what re-runs
- `orca flow edit <run> --step <step> [--file <file>] [--set <set>]` — the person's own output for a step (record fields, or workspace files); the step is not re-run
- `orca flow plan <run>` — compute and propose a re-run plan from what changed (spends one single call)
- `orca flow rerun <run> [--skip <skip>] [--add <add>] [--plan <plan>]` — run the open plan: its candidates minus the skips (default: the model's proposed skips) plus additions; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow discard-plan <run> [--plan <plan>]` — withdraw the open plan instead of running it: nothing re-runs, the feedback that made it is excluded; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow rewind <run> --to <to> [--exclude <exclude>]` — move a step's active output back (to execution n, or to not run); later messages are re-applied unless excluded
- `orca flow revise <run> --step <step> --round <round> --file <file>` — revise an answered round of a flow clarify step; later rounds are asked again from it
- `orca flow include <run> --step <step> [--plan <plan>]` — run a step the running plan asks about (it spends); needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow accept <run> --step <step> [--plan <plan>]` — accept a step of the running plan as unchanged: its output stands for its new inputs (what the timeout does)
- `orca flow skip <run> --step <step>` — skip a step in this run until filled: later steps go on without its output; taken at the next step boundary, so read the run (orca flow journal) to see if it applied
- `orca flow defer <run> --step <step> [--effects <effects>]` — defer a step (fill it later): later steps go on without its output; external effects after it wait unless --effects <step>=proceed (proceed needs a person token); taken at the next step boundary, so read the run (orca flow journal) to see if it applied
- `orca flow fill <run> --step <step>` — fill a skipped or deferred step: a plan re-runs it and what depends on it; taken at the next step boundary, so read the run (orca flow journal) to see if it applied
- `orca flow params <run> --set <set>` — change the run's params mid-run (values folder-relative); changed steps become plan candidates
- `orca flow pause <run>` — pause the run at its next step boundary (a running step is never interrupted)
- `orca flow resume <run>` — resume a paused run
- `orca flow stop <run>` — stop the run for good at its next step boundary
- `orca flow retry <run> --step <step>` — run a failed step again (an effect step's retry makes a new effect record)
- `orca flow repin <run> --version <version>` — move the run to another version of its template (changed steps become plan candidates)
- `orca flow answer <run> [<step>] [--feedback <feedback>] [--set <set>] [--file <file>] [--text <text>] [--answer <answer>] [--glossary <glossary>] [--adr <adr>] [--consensus]` — answer a step that waits for the person (an ask's form, a step's question, a clarify round, or consensus) or a feedback's clarify round; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca flow effect confirm <record>` — confirm an effect card: its step runs now (needs a person token) (person token)
- `orca flow effect enact <record>` — enact a staged effect record: its step runs now (needs a person token) (person token)
- `orca flow effect discard <record>` — discard a staged effect record: the step never runs (needs a person token) (person token)
- `orca flow pool raise <run> --tokens <tokens>` — raise a run's token pool; steps parked on an exhausted pool start again (needs a person token) (person token)

### `orca plan`

- `orca plan list [--archived]` — this project's plan library: entries, their newest version and the schedules that use them
- `orca plan show <entry> [--version <version>]` — a library entry with every version's provenance (by, via, origin, time); --version adds that version's document
- `orca plan save [--group <group>] [--requirement <requirement>] [--draft <draft>] [--name <name>] [--entry <entry>]` — save a group's plan, or a requirement's split draft, to the plan library (--entry appends a version: person token)
- `orca plan import <path> [--name <name>] [--entry <entry>]` — import a plan file (orca-plan-v1, or a scheduler plan file whose contracts are inlined) into this project's library; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca plan export <entry> [--version <version>] --out <out>` — write a library version's orca-plan-v1 bytes to a new file (mode 0600; an existing path is refused)
- `orca plan archive <entry>` — hide a library entry from lists (refused while a schedule uses it)
- `orca plan preview <path>` — print the plan's write sets, conflicts and layering, and the runtime preflight; execute nothing (--verbose: more)

### `orca schedule`

- `orca schedule list [--all]` — this project's schedules: kind, cron, next three slots, last fire and newer-version information
- `orca schedule show <schedule>` — one schedule's body and revision, its next three slots, last fire and newer-version information
- `orca schedule fires <schedule> [--limit <limit>]` — one schedule's fires, newest first: slot, outcome, reason and what it started
- `orca schedule add flow <template> --cron <cron> [--param <param>] [--clarify <clarify>] [--unattended] [--pool <pool>] [--name <name>] [--disabled] [--id <id>]` — a builtin flow template on a cron (at most hourly), at the version the build ships; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca schedule add group <entry> --version <version> --cron <cron> [--token-limit <token-limit>] [--name <name>] [--disabled] [--id <id>]` — a plan library entry at one explicit version on a cron; --version is required (orca plan show lists an entry's versions); needs a person token (person token)
- `orca schedule edit <schedule> [--cron <cron>] [--param <param>] [--name <name>] [--repin <repin>] [--pool <pool>] [--token-limit <token-limit>] [--unlimited]` — change a schedule's cron or name, a flow's params and pool, or a group's pinned version and token limit; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca schedule enable <schedule>` — turn a schedule's fires on; needs a person token (person token)
- `orca schedule disable <schedule>` — turn a schedule's fires off (its row and fires stay)
- `orca schedule remove <schedule>` — mark a schedule removed: it never fires again and frees its place in the limit
- `orca schedule resume <schedule>` — resume a schedule paused after repeated failed starts

### `orca dev`

- `orca dev gate --hook <hook>` — Tier 0 gate: read a Claude Code PreToolUse hook's JSON on stdin; exit 2 with one line on stderr when the Bash command would push, merge into main, delete a branch or remove a worktree, or when it cannot decide
- `orca dev level --hook <hook>` — context level: read a Claude Code PostToolUse hook's JSON on stdin and print the reading (and a checkpoint request past T1) as additional context
- `orca dev checkpoint write [--repo <repo>] --session <session> [--transcript <transcript>] --draft <draft>` — write and commit a checkpoint for this session from a draft file outside the repository
- `orca dev resume [--repo <repo>] [--checkpoint <checkpoint>]` — print the latest checkpoint and re-run the shell commands it recorded
- `orca dev chain start --repo <repo> [--by <by>] --goal <goal> --max-sessions <max-sessions> --max-cost-usd <max-cost-usd> [--session-timeout-min <session-timeout-min>] [--chain-id <chain-id>] [--via <via>]` — start an unattended chain of sessions toward --goal under four hard limits
- `orca dev chain stop --repo <repo> [--chain-id <chain-id>]` — ask the running chain to stop after its current session ends
- `orca dev chain unlock --repo <repo>` — after checking its supervisor is gone: remove a chain's lock and record the chain as stopped (unlocked-by-human)
- `orca dev check-append-only` — read a git diff on stdin; refuse it if it deletes any line
- `orca dev correct [--decision <decision>] [--kind <kind>] [--because <because>] [--repo <repo>] [--by <by>] [--chose-instead <chose-instead>] [--undo-how <undo-how>] [--undo-cost <undo-cost>] [--undo-blast-radius <undo-blast-radius>] [--close <close>] [--again] [--record-only]` — offline ledger writer: record a correction of a decision; with --chose-instead/--undo-how also close the loop (writes and commits the two ledger rows)

### `orca control`

- `orca control get <path>` — read one control path over the socket: get <path> [--control-state-dir <dir>] [--client-name <name>]
- `orca control send <route>` — send one control command: send <route> --expected-revision <n> (--payload <json> | --payload-file <file>) [--command-id <id>]

Escape-hatch only (no command; `orca control send`): `shutdown`, `system-debug-open`.

# Orca

_Leave it to Orca — every idea, made real._

Orca is subsystem C of the A′ decision-ledger design: a scheduler that runs a
plan of tasks over ccloop (a sibling repository), reconciles their results
against a shared work branch, and records every scheduling and reconciliation
choice it makes into an append-only decision ledger (`.decisions/*.jsonl`).

## `orca plan preview`

```
orca plan preview <path> [--verbose]
```

`orca plan preview` reads a plan file, computes every task's write set, builds the
task graph, layers it, and prints a report — write sets, intersecting pairs,
layers, and any up-front rejections. It touches nothing in the target
repository beyond read-only git calls (`git rev-parse`, `git status
--porcelain`) — no branch is created, no commit is made, no ref moves.

Rounds run through the panel (`orca panel`) and its control path; `orca plan preview`
previews a round.

### The plan file's shape

```jsonc
{
  "targetRepo": "/absolute/path/to/the/repo/orca/schedules",
  "ccloopBin": "/absolute/path/to/ccloop/dist/cli.js",
  "runsDir": "/absolute/path/outside/targetRepo/for/run/copies",
  "workBranch": "orca/w/some-round",
  "policy": "local-merge",
  "ledgerMode": "in-repo",
  "tasks": [
    { "taskId": "T1", "contract": "/absolute/path/to/T1-contract.json", "dependsOn": [] },
    { "taskId": "T2", "contract": "/absolute/path/to/T2-contract.json", "dependsOn": ["T1"] }
  ]
}
```

- `targetRepo` — the repository the round lands work into. Orca checks this
  repository's own worktree out onto `workBranch` and merges into it; it
  never touches the base branch it cut `workBranch` from.
- `ccloopBin` — ccloop's `dist/cli.js`, spawned as a subprocess (ccloop's
  `package.json` is `private: true` and its `bin` is never an npm
  dependency).
- `runsDir` — outside `targetRepo`, where each task's throwaway clone and any
  escalation files live.
- `workBranch` — the branch every task's result is merged into (`W`). It is
  cut from **the branch the target repository currently has checked out** —
  Orca does not resolve the repository's true default branch, so running it
  while sitting on `feature/x` cuts `W` from `feature/x`. It must not already
  exist and must not be that base branch.
- `ledgerMode` — `"in-repo"` is implemented. `"out-of-repo"` is accepted by
  the schema (spec §8.5) but rejected at run time with exit 1, the same
  treatment an unsupported `policy` value gets: recognised but not yet
  built, refused loudly rather than silently downgraded.
- `tasks[].contract` — every contract file must live outside `targetRepo`
  (one of the up-front rejections below); Orca reads it as opaque,
  unvalidated JSON and derives each task's write set from
  `context.targetPaths ∪ safetyPolicy.allowlistPaths`.

### The up-front rejections

Seven are evaluated purely from the plan file's own content, before any git
call is made against the target repository. (Spec §9.1(4) counts nine
altogether; `unusable-task-id` was added by the final whole-branch review as
a seventh plan-level check, so the count is now ten — recorded here as an
erratum against the spec's number rather than left to be discovered.)

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `relative-path` | a path field (`ccloopBin`, `runsDir`, a task's `contract`) is not absolute |
| `duplicate-task-id` | two tasks in the plan share a `taskId` |
| `cycle` | the task graph (explicit `dependsOn` plus implicit write-set edges) has a cycle |
| `contract-inside-target-repo` | a task's contract file lives inside `targetRepo` |
| `work-branch-is-default` | `workBranch` names the base branch (the one the target repository currently has checked out) |
| `unsupported-policy` | `policy` is anything other than `"local-merge"` |
| `unusable-task-id` | a `taskId` cannot become a run id (spec §2.1 derives `orca-<taskId>-<hash8>`, and the ledger requires `/^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$/`) |

An eighth plan-level rejection, `unreadable-contract`, is reported the same
way and at the same point: a task's `contract` path that cannot be read, or
whose content is not valid JSON. It is not in the table above because it is
not decidable from the plan file's own bytes — it needs one `readFile` per
task.

Three more are runtime checks — a read-only `git rev-parse` or `git status
--porcelain` against the target repository, which does not count as
"touching" it, so `orca plan preview` evaluates these for real too, not just
a running round:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `work-branch-already-exists` | `workBranch` already exists in the target repository |
| `base-not-a-commit` | the base branch does not resolve to a real commit yet |
| `dirty-worktree` | the target repository's worktree has uncommitted changes, or its cleanliness cannot be read at all (`targetRepo` is not a git repository) |

A plan file that fails to parse at all (malformed JSON, or the wrong shape)
is reported as `malformed` and is not one of these — it means there is no
plan to evaluate them against yet.

Any rejection, plan-level or runtime, makes `orca plan preview` and a round
exit 1 (spec §9.3). A *warning* — a plan that is legal but fully serial, say
— does not affect the exit code.

### What Web import also requires

The panel's **Import plan** (Task control) reads the same file and adds its own checks. It accepts a plan only when:

- `targetRepo` is the repository the plan is registered for (`--plan <planId>=<repoId>=<path>`);
- the plan has a `goal`;
- the plan has at least one `successConditions` entry, and no two are identical;
- every task has a `targetVersion` that is a positive integer (write `1` unless you mean otherwise);
- no task lists a dependency twice or depends on a task that is not in the plan;
- every task's `contract` file is valid JSON in ccloop's contract format (or its `loop` block is valid).

A plan that fails is refused with `control-plan-rejected`, listing every problem it can see at once, one per line:
`target-repo-mismatch`, `missing-goal`, `missing-success-conditions`, `duplicate-success-condition`, then per task
`duplicate-dependency:<task>`, `dangling-dependency:<task>`, `missing-target-version:<task>` and the task's contract
problem (`contract-json:<task>`, `contract-shape:<task>`, `contract-canonical:<task>`, `loop-plan-invalid:<task>:<reason>`).
A file that does not match the schema at all is refused with its `malformed:<path>: <message>` lines alone. The panel
explains each line in English or Chinese.

### Exit codes

Every task and every round-level event contributes one of four values, and
the round's exit code is whichever contribution is the most severe, in the
order **3 > 2 > 1 > 0**:

- **0** — nothing failed and nothing needed a human. The round completed
  cleanly.
- **1** — the round was refused before it started: an unreadable or
  malformed plan file, an unimplemented
  `ledgerMode`, a repository lock that could not be acquired (another `orca`
  process already holds it), or any of the up-front rejections above.
- **2** — an ordinary failure, or a decision that was still safe to make on
  its own: a task's net change set was empty (`succeeded_but_empty`), a task
  failed or exhausted its attempts, or a task landed despite writing outside
  its declared write set but touched nobody else's declared claims (a
  tier-1 `boundary` decision, recorded in the ledger).
- **3** — an escalation: a human has to come back and look. This covers an
  out-of-bounds write that collides with a sibling task's declared write set
  in the same layer, a merge conflict whose reconciliation could not be
  synthesized or verified, a task ccloop reports `blocked_waiting_human`
  (which is a terminal, non-resumable state in ccloop — not something Orca
  retries), or an exception that escaped the round entirely.

### The escalation file

Whenever a round contributes exit code 3 for a reason that has both sides'
intent and conflict blocks to report — a merge conflict Orca could not
reconcile automatically, or a task that wrote outside its declared write set
into a path a sibling task also declared — Orca writes
`<runsDir>/escalations/<runId>.md` and prints its path. It contains, in this
order: why a human has to look, what each side's contract declared as its
goal and success condition, the conflicted paths or blocks, and an
executable `undo.how`/cost/blast-radius for cleaning up the kept copies. It
is written under `runsDir`, never onto the work branch — the work branch is
a code branch, and this is a process file for a human, not a decision to
bind a commit to.

A round that escalates because a task reported `blocked_waiting_human` gets
**no** escalation file: the file's mandated content — both sides' intent and
the conflict blocks — does not exist for a single task that is simply
waiting on a person, so there is nothing honest to put in one. The round
still contributes exit code 3, keeps the task's copy, and prints where it
is.

## `orca dev correct`

```
orca dev correct --decision <run-id>/<n> --kind wrong|not_my_taste|stale --because <text>
             [--repo <path>] [--by <who>] [--again] [--record-only]
             [--chose-instead <text> --undo-how <text> [--undo-cost <text>] [--undo-blast-radius <text>]]
orca dev correct --close <correctionId> --undo-how <text> [--repo <path>] [--chose-instead <text>]
```

A correction records a human overturning a past decision. There are two
modes:

- **Record-only** — write the correction into the corrections store and stop
  there. This is what happens when neither `--chose-instead` nor
  `--undo-how` is given, or when `--record-only` is passed explicitly (which
  forces record-only even if `--chose-instead` is given alongside it, for
  the case where the alternative is already known but the undo plan is
  not). `--decision` names the decision being corrected
  (`<run-id>/<n>`, the same id a `decision` ledger row carries); `--again`
  says "yes, record a second correction against the same decision by the
  same person on purpose" — without it, a repeat is refused rather than
  silently duplicated. `--by` defaults to `git config user.name`.
- **Closing the loop** — giving *either* `--chose-instead` or `--undo-how`
  expresses the intent to close, and then both are required (a typo in one
  no longer silently falls back to record-only). Closing derives two rows —
  a new `decision` and an `overturned` referencing the one it replaces —
  writes them to the target repository's `.decisions/orca-fix-<hash8>.jsonl`
  in one append, and commits just that one file on the branch the repository
  currently has checked out, leaving the rest of the person's staging area
  untouched.
- **`--close <correctionId>`** re-opens the closing half of a correction that
  was already recorded (by a prior record-only run, or by a `--close` that
  landed the ledger rows but failed to commit — see exit 5 below). It cannot
  be combined with `--decision`, `--kind`, `--because`, or `--again` — those
  already live on the stored row — and `--chose-instead` may only supply a
  value the stored row is missing, not override one it already has.

Running the same closing command twice is safe: the second run recognises
the correction is already recorded (or already committed) and refuses or
no-ops rather than writing a second `overturned` row into the append-only
ledger.

### Exit codes

- **0** — the correction was recorded, or the loop was closed and committed
  (including the no-op case: this exact correction was already closed).
- **1** — the input was refused: bad or missing arguments, an unknown
  `--decision`, a correction already recorded (without `--again`), a
  `--close` argument conflict, the target repository mid-merge/rebase/
  cherry-pick or on a detached HEAD, or any other named rejection — the
  message says which.
- **3** — an exception nobody anticipated (the same top-level handler `orca
  plan` uses).
- **4** — another `orca` process holds the target repository's lock;
  transient, retry later.
- **5** — the ledger rows landed on disk and were staged, but the commit
  itself was refused (e.g. a hook rejected it); re-run the exact same
  `--close` command to finish just the commit, without writing the rows a
  second time.

This scale is `orca dev correct`'s own — it does not reuse `orca plan preview`'s and
a round's 0/1/2/3. `orca decision validate` has a separate scale of its own too: 0 (all
ledger files ok), 1 (a file was rejected or none were found), and 2 (a
decision was downgraded to tier 0 — legal, but not an agent's to decide).

### The corrections store

Corrections live outside any git repository, by design — the point of a
correction is to feed a memory layer that spans repositories, not to be
another line item in one repository's ledger. By default the store is
`~/.orca/corrections.jsonl`; set `ORCA_CORRECTIONS_DIR` to redirect it to a
different directory (its file is always named `corrections.jsonl` inside
that directory). A directory or file this program creates for the first
time is created `0700`/`0600` respectively, never inherited from the
process's umask; a directory or file that already exists keeps whatever
mode it has — that is a person's data, and this program does not get to
change it.

## Known gaps (spec §10.4)

These are registered, not hidden, straight from the design's own accounting:

1. The `scripted` adapter means v1 has not verified how accurate a real
   agent's declarations are. What v1 verifies is a structural property (the
   system stays correct even when a write-set criterion is wrong), not
   whether criteria are accurate.
2. Layer-by-layer progress means the slowest task in a layer blocks the
   whole layer (dispatching as soon as a task is ready is a pure
   optimisation and does not change criteria semantics).
3. The work branch's base is read once, at round start, from the HEAD of
   whatever branch the target repository has checked out; a long-running
   round does not pick up updates to that branch made while it runs.
   Resolving the repository's *true* default branch (rather than using the
   checked-out one) is registered as post-v1 work.
4. Escalation is terminal — there is no incremental resume. A human who
   resolves an escalation reruns the whole plan, and every task that already
   finished runs again for nothing. Harmless while v1 spends nothing
   (`scripted` adapter); the leading candidate for post-v1 work.
5. Until the corresponding change lands in ccloop (see §4.4), the patch path
   has three channels that can silently collapse into an empty patch.
6. As long as that change has not landed, §7's second direction (declared
   but not produced) degrades to "is the patch empty or not."
7. There is no "stop just one task" — orca has no way to end one task and
   let the round continue. (The reason given here used to be that
   `cancelled` only comes from a signal to the whole process group. That is
   incomplete, measured 2026-09-05: ccloop also returns `cancelled` when the
   verification's `stopSignals` meet the contract's `escalationAndExit.stopOn`,
   which is per-contract and is how `cancelledRound.test.ts` produces a real
   one. It is still not a handle orca holds — the signal comes from the
   task's own verification — so the limitation stands and its reason does
   not.)
8. `ledgerMode: out-of-repo` inherits the weakness A′ §3.7 already
   acknowledges about itself: it has no immutable anchor.
9. The shell does not distinguish between exit codes 1, 2, and 3 — to a
   shell they are all simply "non-zero."
10. Squash-commit detection is a heuristic, not a proof.
11. The reasons worktree-based approaches were rejected are reasoning, not
   measurement (and do not need to be measured).
12. The `--serial` consistency criterion (S10) runs the entire plan twice —
   it is a v1 criterion, not a production switch.

## Contributing to `.decisions/`

Day to day — iterations, fix rounds, merges into `main`, push, installing the
panel service — `npm test` runs only the tests a change touches
(`scripts/test-affected.mjs`: it prints every selected file with its reason,
always runs the typecheck, and says so when it selects zero); `npm run test:all`
runs the whole root suite. `npm run verify` is the release gate: it refuses
(exit 2) unless the human asked for a tagged release
(`ORCA_RELEASE_TAG=<tag> npm run verify`), then runs typecheck, build, the
whole root suite once (with formal control verification and a chain session's
variables), ledger validation, the CLAUDE.md line-count check, the hooks-path
check, the web build, the ccloop pin and panel checks, and the workspace
checks. The pre-commit hook (`scripts/githooks/pre-commit`) is deliberately narrower: it
only re-checks `.decisions/**` for append-only violations when a commit
actually touches that directory, which is why it stays fast regardless of
how large `npm run verify` grows.

## Checkpoint handoff (subsystem D, v1: Claude Code)

A development session in this repository learns its own context-window level from a `PostToolUse` hook
(`.claude/settings.json` runs `orca dev level --hook claude-code`). At T1 (330,000 tokens by default) it is told to
write a checkpoint; past T2 (450,000) it is told to hand off; when the level cannot be read it is told so on every call.

- `orca dev checkpoint write --session <id> --transcript <path> --draft <file>` writes and commits
  `.orca/checkpoints/<run-id>.json`. The agent's draft carries judgment only (next steps, open items, what waits
  for a human, which commands to measure); the level, HEAD and every measurement's exit code are measured by the command.
- `orca dev resume` starts the next session from the latest checkpoint reachable from HEAD and re-measures everything
  that may have changed, including publish state from `git ls-remote`.
- Thresholds and model window sizes can be set in `.orca/level.json`; that file lives in the repository and is
  unrelated to the per-user `~/.orca` store.

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-17-checkpoint-handoff-design.md`.

## Tier 0 gate

A `PreToolUse` hook (`.claude/settings.json`, `Bash` matcher) runs every Bash
command in this repository's Claude Code sessions through
`scripts/gate-prefilter.mjs` and, when that does not resolve it, `orca dev gate
--hook claude-code`. It blocks four irreversible git/gh moves — `git push`,
`git branch -d`/`-D`/`--delete`, `git worktree remove`/`prune`, and `gh pr
merge`/`gh repo sync` — plus any non-`GET` `gh api` call, whether typed
directly or through `rtk`/`rtk proxy`. It also blocks a merge into `main`:
on `main` this means `git merge`, `git pull`, `git rebase` and any `git
reset` that moves HEAD; whatever the current branch, it also means `git
branch -f`/`-M`/`-m`/`-C`/`-c … main`, `git checkout -B main`, `git switch
-C main`, a `git fetch` refspec ending in `:main`, and `git update-ref
refs/heads/main`. `permissions.deny` backs only the
eight literal move patterns above (each also in `rtk `/`rtk proxy ` form) at
the literal-string layer, ahead of the hook — it has no entry for `gh api`
(its arbitrary flags can't be enumerated as literal prefixes) and none for a
merge into main, so those, and any non-literal form of the moves above, rest
on the hook alone.

A blocked move is not lost: do it in your own terminal, outside the agent
session. `orca dev resume` and `orca dev checkpoint write` refuse to record a
measurement the gate blocked, exiting with `measurement-gated` rather than
recording a false pass.

`permissions.deny` matches literal prefixes only. The hook is different: it
parses the command — quoting, command substitution, heredocs, `sh -c` and
the like — and errs toward blocking when it cannot decide. What still gets
through is narrower and more deliberate: a command written into a script
file, an inline interpreter invocation such as `python3 -c "…"`, or `rm -rf`
of a worktree directory. See residual risks in
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-18-tier0-gate-design.md` §7.

## Unattended chains (`orca dev chain`)

`orca dev chain start --repo <path> --by <you> --goal <text> --max-sessions <n> --max-cost-usd <x>` runs headless Claude
Code sessions one after another in `<path>` — a dedicated clone or worktree of an Orca checkout, whose Tier 0 gate
wiring must equal `src/gate/settings.ts`. Each session starts from `orca dev resume` and ends by writing an exit checkpoint
(`"chain": {"status": "continue" | "done" | "blocked", "why": "..."}`); code, not the model, decides whether the next
session starts. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 refused before anything was written, 2 an anomaly (a changed gate or guarded
path, a dirty worktree, rewritten history, a timeout, no exit checkpoint, an unreadable cost, ...), 3 everything left
waits for a person, 4 a limit or a stop request.

- The target needs `node_modules/.bin/tsx` (a fresh worktree often has no `node_modules`: link or install it first);
  otherwise the start is refused with `tsx-missing`.
- The model and the default session timeout (360 minutes, a backstop) come from `.orca/chain.json`, e.g.
  `{"model": "claude-opus-5[1m]"}`; `orca dev level` must know that model's window. The cost limit is soft.
- The record `.orca/chains/<chain-id>.json` is committed on its own after every session; raw session output is in the
  ignored `.orca/chain-logs/`. The chain lock and stop requests live in the git dir.
- `orca dev chain stop --repo <path>` stops the chain after its current session; `orca dev chain unlock --repo <path>` clears
  the lock of a supervisor that is gone and records the chain as stopped.
- The panel shows each repository's latest chain, starts and stops chains, and shows a banner when one stops
  (dismissing it is remembered in the browser only). Anyone holding the panel token can start a paid, unattended agent
  that commits: see the D-launch spec §7.

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-18-d-launch-design.md`.


## Durable task control foundation

`src/control` provides an opt-in, single-host SQLite control service (Node.js
22.13.1 or newer). It persists group/work identities, idempotent claims,
work/handoff budget reservations, cumulative usage, dispatch intents, independent
archives and committed checkpoints. A recovered writer reconciles existing run
identities before dispatch can resume. Unknown execution or missing evidence keeps
the run blocked and its remaining budget reserved. Copying a state directory does
not transfer execution ownership; host and canonical-path checks reject copies.

This slice is a foundation. The production ccloop control protocol is not yet
implemented: the production factory refuses execution and has no legacy adapter
fallback. Offline protocol peers exist only under tests. There is no new Web stop
or resume promise, and this does not upgrade Codex soft budgets to hard limits.
The existing CLI retains its legacy execution path.

`ControlService.run(groupId, planPath, options)` verifies the approved graph and
uses the shared scheduler. A service is bound to an explicit `targetRepo`; the
logical `projectKey` is not a filesystem path. Reconciliation requires an explicit
`reconcileGrant` and uses only the group's remaining approved budget. Agent-specific
adaptation belongs in ccloop. The prepared start envelope and raw evidence reader
are the protocol seam for that follow-up.

Evidence consumers use `listGroupArtifacts(store, groupId)` or
`listTaskArtifacts(store, groupId, taskId)`, then `readArtifact(store, ref)` to read
and independently verify the archived bytes. Checkpoint authority comes from
`readCommittedCheckpoint`, never a scanned `latest.json` file. Cleanup requires a
committed recoverable checkpoint, retained raw evidence, an unchanged source
directory identity, and confirmed landing for successful work. Recovery retries
only cleanup that was already durably authorized and never re-executes a merge.
A claim without a prepared dispatch intent remains blocked for explicit recovery.

Run the offline control gate by name with `npm run verify:control`. `npm run verify`
no longer runs it as a separate pass: its single suite pass sets `ORCA_CONTROL_VERIFY=1`
and refuses up front when `ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` or `ORCA_AGENTS_TABLE` is unset or
unresolvable (`scripts/check-gate-env.mjs`). Scheduler integration tests require the existing ccloop build
through `ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` when the checkout has no sibling ccloop repository.
The round criteria in `tests/scheduler` need a ccloop checkout (the sibling `../ccloop`, or
`ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` pointing at a checkout's `dist/cli.js`) at or after the ccloop commit titled
`test(fixtures): fake codex plays scripted frames per attempt, for callers leaving --adapter scripted`:
they run that checkout's `tests/fixtures/fake-codex.mjs`, which the pinned ccloop package does not ship.

`orca panel` and `orca agent` find ccloop through `ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` when it is set
(an empty value means "no execution port"), and otherwise through a ccloop package
installed in Orca's `node_modules` (Orca's `package.json` is meant to pin it to a commit
by git URL -- see the human step in
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-29-ccloop-git-dependency.md`, Task 5). With neither,
`orca agent` stops with `ccloop-not-installed` and the panel starts without an
execution port. The real-ccloop criteria under `tests/control` and
`npm run verify:control` still need `ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` pointing at a ccloop checkout's
build, because they use fixtures from ccloop's `tests/` tree, which the package does
not ship. `ORCA_CCLOOP_DEFAULT_E2E=1` (with `ORCA_CCLOOP_BIN` unset) runs
`tests/control/ccloopDefaultE2E.test.ts` against the installed package.

## Memory section (read-only)

`orca panel` shows a Memory section when `ORCA_CCMEM_BIN` is an absolute path to the ccmem executable. It reads
with `ccmem export --json --scope global` and then `--scope project`, in the repository's directory, so ccmem
computes the project key itself. Nothing is written by Orca. Opening the section starts ccmem, and ccmem may migrate
its own data root when it opens it (backup copy and pruning; spec `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-29-memory-tab-design.md` §4).
Unset, the section says it is not configured and ccmem is never started. A repository without a git remote may show
no project memory: ccmem keys such a project by the session's directory, which may differ from the repository root.
